strengths: Introduces Clean-PR, a large-scale verified PR corpus (2M+ instances, 12 languages) with rigorous filtering, issue linking, and Search/Replace conversion plus round-trip verification, addressing a real data gap for repository-level code editing.

Provides a clear two-stage training recipe (mid-training followed by Agentless-aligned SFT with error-driven augmentation) and demonstrates substantial SWE-bench gains (24.3% Lite, 30.6% Verified) over strong baselines including a StarCoder2-style dataset and Qwen-Coder-32B-Instruct.

Ablations isolate key design choices, showing that verified Search/Replace blocks outperform unified diffs, linked-issue context helps, and error-driven augmentation improves both localization and end-to-end repair.

Shows positive transfer to general code benchmarks (HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) and Pass@k scaling, suggesting the data does not cause catastrophic forgetting and leaves room for verifier/reranking gains.
The paper is generally well written and includes useful appendices on data construction, decontamination, prompts, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The multi-language benefit claim is confounded by token count: the Python-only model uses 3.8B tokens while the All-Languages model uses 17.7B tokens, so the improvement cannot be attributed to language diversity without a token-matched comparison.

Potential contamination or overlap between the SFT data (SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym) and SWE-bench evaluation is not adequately addressed; decontamination is described for the mid-training corpus but not clearly for the SFT trajectories.

There is an inconsistency about the StarCoder2-style baseline: Section 3.1 and Table 8 describe it as using 'PR Desc Only', while Appendix B.3 says linked issues are aggregated into the baseline, leaving it unclear what was actually compared.
Text and table disagree on a key number: Section 3.2 states Base+SFT achieves 10.3% on Lite, but Table 6 reports 11.3%.
The external comparison in Table 7 lists Lingma-SWE and SWE-Fixer with identical scores (22.0/30.2) and identical parameter counts, which appears erroneous and weakens the external baseline analysis.
No statistical significance or variance is reported across training seeds; SWE-bench Lite and Verified are fixed evaluation sets, so the robustness of the reported gains is unclear.

Reproducibility and ethical treatment of the dataset release are underexplored: the paper promises to release repository URLs, PR descriptions, and comments without a concrete license-filtering or PII-anonymization plan for Clean-PR, raising licensing and privacy concerns.
Evaluation is limited to a single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) and one scaffold (Agentless), so the claim that the learned repository alignment is methodology-agnostic is not tested.
Some key metrics such as File Acc. and Line Acc. are not precisely defined, and no code or model release is mentioned, which limits full reproducibility.
The abstract and Table 1 are inconsistent about corpus scale: the abstract claims a 2M-PR corpus while Clean-PR-full is reported as 3.05M instances, and the release scope is unclear.

strengths: Well-engineered data pipeline: the noise taxonomy, PR validity filtering, issue linking via regex, and especially the round-trip (Search/Replace re-application) verification that discards any block not bit-wise reconstructing the target state, are thoughtful and reproducible in principle.
Genuine scale and multilingual scope (16.4M raw PRs filtered to ~3M Clean-PR-full, 2M Clean-PR-train, 12 languages, 17.7B tokens), which is a useful resource if actually released.

Evaluation goes beyond a single number: valid-patch rate plus intermediate file/line localisation metrics, and ablations isolating edit format (Diff vs S/R), issue augmentation, and error-driven augmentation (Tables 6, 8, 9).
The catastrophic-forgetting analysis (Figure 2) is a sensible addition, showing HumanEval/LiveCodeBench are preserved rather than degraded by the proposed mid-training.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the Search/Replace edit format and the Agentless localisation→navigation→editing decomposition are taken directly from Xia et al. (2025); mid-training on PR/commit data closely mirrors StarCoder2/CommitPack. The novel component reduces largely to data curation, which is a better fit for a dataset/benchmark track than ICML main track.

The headline multi-language claim is unsupported by evaluation. All results are on SWE-bench Lite/Verified, which are Python-only. The assertion that Java/C++/Go exposure improves abstract reasoning is inferred solely from Python scores and would require Multi-SWE-bench or SWE-PolyBench to substantiate.

External comparison (Table 7) is not apples-to-apples and appears erroneous: Lingma-SWE and SWE-Fixer are reported with identical numbers (22.0/30.2), which is a red flag for a copy/paste or data error; and SWE-Gym is compared under a different scaffold (OpenHands) than the Agentless protocol used here, so 'significantly outperforms' is misleading.
Internal numerical inconsistency: the text states Base+SFT reaches '10.3% on Lite', while Table 6 reports 11.3%. Small but symptomatic of insufficient care.

No variance, seed, or significance reporting. Pass@1 gaps of 1–3% across several rows (e.g., Python vs All, Standard vs Error-Aug) are presented as meaningful without any estimate of run-to-run noise.

Confounded main comparison: the StarCoder2-style baseline differs from Clean-PR simultaneously in edit format, filtering policy, and issue augmentation; the ablation (Table 8) only partially disentangles these, so the source of the +10-point Verified gap is not cleanly attributed.

Reproducibility is limited: 32×H200 training for ~259h, dependence on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct as the augmentation noise generator (same scale as the trained model), and neither the dataset nor the checkpoint is verifiably available to reviewers. The SFT stage reuses SWE-rebench/SWE-Gym (SWE-bench-adjacent distributions), which risks inflating test-set results and confounds the claimed benefit of the mid-training stage.

Presentation/proofreading defects that undermine confidence: an obviously garbled '.邮件' (Chinese for 'email') extension appears in the allowed-extension table (Table 12), and phrasing such as 'besides heavy inference scaffolding' / 'besides requiring heavy agent scaffolding' is grammatically wrong (should be 'without').

strengths: The paper contributes a large, publicly-released, verified PR corpus (2M instances, 17.7B tokens, 12 languages) with a concrete reconstruction-and-validation pipeline (round-trip application with bit-wise equality check) that meaningfully raises data quality over naive diff ingestion; the noise statistics in Table 2 and the pipeline in Algorithm 1 are transparent and reproducible.

The empirical results are substantial and consistently favor the proposed recipe: absolute gains of 13.6% on SWE-bench Lite and 12.3% on Verified over the instruct baseline, with improved Valid Patch, File, and Line metrics (Table 6). The ablation in Table 8 cleanly isolates the contributions of Search/Replace format vs. Unified Diff and of linked-issue context vs. PR-description-only, and Table 9 isolates the error-driven augmentation.

The paper provides a useful finding beyond the headline number: verified Search/Replace mid-training shows positive transfer to general coding (HumanEval 54.1→59.8, LiveCodeBench 29.0→32.6), while the diff-based StarCoder2-style baseline degrades (Figure 2). This addresses catastrophic forgetting directly rather than ignoring it.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: full training hyperparameters (Table 17), the exact data-format template (Table 15), inference prompts for all three Agentless stages (Tables 18–20), a detailed dataset schema (Table 16), and a multi-layer decontamination protocol (Appendix A.6) are provided.

The positioning relative to agentic scaffolding is well-motivated and the framing of the research question (how much repo-editing capability can be internalized into weights) is coherent and useful for the community.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) and two closely related benchmarks (SWE-bench Lite/Verified). Given the paper's emphasis on 12-language training, there is no evaluation on the multilingual benchmarks it cites (Multi-SWE-bench, SWE-PolyBench), so the central multi-language claim is supported only by two English/Python-dominated splits.

There are consistency errors in the reported comparisons. Table 7 lists identical scores (Lite 22.0, Verified 30.2) for two distinct 72B methods (Lingma-SWE and SWE-Fixer), which is suspicious and undermines the external comparison. Additionally, Section 3.2 states the Base+SFT model achieves '10.3% on Lite' while Table 6 reports 11.3%, and the concluding sentence ('besides requiring heavy agent scaffolding') appears to invert the intended meaning.

Potential train/test contamination is not fully ruled out for the SFT stage. The Agentless-aligned SFT data is drawn from SWE-rebench and SWE-Gym, whose tasks overlap in distribution with SWE-bench; the decontamination protocol (Appendix A.6) is described primarily for the mid-training corpus, and it is not made explicit whether the SFT trajectories were decontaminated against the Lite/Verified gold patches and issue descriptions.

The gains attributed to error-driven augmentation are modest (e.g., Lite 21.8→24.3) and reported on small evaluation sets (300/500 instances) without any significance testing or variance estimates, making it hard to judge whether the effect is robust rather than within noise. The Best-of-N results (Figure 3) further suggest the ranking objective, not the model's intrinsic capability, is a large bottleneck, which weakens the strength of the pass@1 claims.

The StarCoder2-style comparison baseline is reconstructed by the authors; while the effort is commendable, it is not guaranteed to match the original StarCoder2 recipe, and no separate ablation isolates the individual filtering decisions (bot filtering, core-language enforcement, issue linking, complexity caps) to show which parts of the pipeline actually drive the gains.

Presentation could be tightened: the impact statement and conclusion contain grammatical issues, and several claims (e.g., 'largest publicly available corpus') rely on the reader trusting the crawl snapshot rather than an auditable count.

strengths: Introduces Clean-PR, a large-scale verified PR corpus (3.05M full, 2.02M train, 12 languages) converted into Search/Replace blocks through round-trip verification, addressing a clear data gap for repository-level code editing.

Rigorous data construction pipeline: bot/noise filtering, core-language constraints, issue linking, deterministic patch validation, and multi-layer decontamination (repository exclusion, SHA-256 matching, n-gram and issue-Jaccard filtering) with a semantic leakage analysis.
Comprehensive evaluation across SWE-bench Lite/Verified, 7B scaling, multilingual Multi-SWE-bench Flash, OpenHands agentic transfer, Pass@k, and HumanEval/LiveCodeBench forgetting analysis.
Ablations isolate the contributions of Search/Replace formatting, linked-issue augmentation, and error-driven augmentation, showing consistent gains over controlled baselines.
Strong empirical results: +13.0 points over Base+SFT on both SWE-bench Lite and Verified, with competitive performance against much larger 72B baselines under the Agentless protocol.
Clear motivation and good reproducibility detail: training hyperparameters, inference prompts, conversion algorithm, data schema, and a concrete data-release plan.

Demonstrates transfer across model scale, programming language, and inference paradigm (Agentless and OpenHands), supporting the central claim that repository-editing ability can be encoded into weights.
weaknesses: Mid-training input includes PR comments (`validcomments`, Table 19), which can contain solution hints (e.g., Table 13: “The .shape access is safer here”). These comments are unavailable at inference, creating privileged-information leakage and a train-test mismatch; no ablation of comments is provided.

No explicit decontamination guarantee is given for the main SFT data (SWE-rebench/SWE-Gym) relative to SWE-bench Lite/Verified; the semantic leakage analysis covers only the Clean-PR mid-training corpus, not the SFT data.
External baseline comparison in Table 7 reports identical numbers for Lingma-SWE and SWE-Fixer (22.0/30.2), which is suspicious and weakens the claim of surpassing 72B baselines.
Missing comparisons to recent PR/synthetic-data training methods (e.g., SWE-smith, SWE-Synth, R2E-Gym) as training baselines, making it difficult to assess the relative advantage of Clean-PR.

Several reproducibility details are underspecified: loss masking during mid-training (whether loss is computed on input code or only on target edits), exact File/Line accuracy definitions, and inference-time handling of large files and context windowing.

The dataset is promised but not yet released, and license-compliance/attribution filtering for Clean-PR is not described, which is a notable ethics and reproducibility concern for a data-centric paper.
No variance estimates, error bars, or statistical significance tests are reported for benchmark results, though the main gains are large enough that this is not fatal.

Presentation issues: a corrupted extension “邮” appears repeatedly in Table 15, the abstract says 2M PRs while the introduction says 3M PRs, and the paper overclaims “publicly available” before release.

The “Agentless-aligned” approach still uses multi-step retrieval, file localisation, navigation, and patch generation, so the claim of reducing reliance on scaffolding is somewhat overstated; the method does not eliminate inference-time scaffolding.

strengths: The data pipeline is described in unusual detail (Algorithm 1, Appendix A.1–A.10, Tables 15/19/20), including round-trip verification via fake-git-apply plus deterministic string replacement, minimal-unique-context expansion, and context windowing. This is engineering that others could plausibly re-implement.

The decontamination protocol is a genuine strength and goes beyond common practice: repository-level exclusion, SHA-256 exact-file matching, 15-gram gold-patch overlap, issue-description Jaccard filtering, and an embedding/FAISS-based semantic leakage analysis (Appendix A.7, Table 16) showing a non-significant negative correlation (r = -0.061, p = 0.184) between train-test similarity and resolve rate.

The gains are consistent across several axes (32B and 7B, Python-only and multi-language, Multi-SWE-bench Flash, and OpenHands CodeActAgent in Table 12), which makes a pure artefact explanation less likely and suggests the PR-derived signal is doing something real.

Table 8 provides a controlled ablation on a fixed token budget (Python subset) that disentangles edit format (S/R vs. Diff) and issue linking, which is the right way to argue for the individual pipeline design choices.

The two-stage recipe (mid-training on verified S/R edits, then Agentless-aligned stepwise SFT with mined hard negatives) is coherent and its SFT data composition is reported (Table 5), and training/inference prompts and hyperparameters are given in Appendix C.
An impact statement is included that at least acknowledges code reliability, misuse, and licensing/attribution concerns.
weaknesses: The evaluation is statistically underpowered for the claims made. Every number is a single run with no seeds, no confidence intervals, and no variance reporting, on benchmarks of 300 (Lite) and 500 (Verified) instances. Differences such as 22.3 vs. 24.3 on Lite (6 instances) or the 2–3 point effects in Tables 8 and 9 are within plausible run-to-run noise, yet the paper draws firm conclusions about format, issue linking, and error-driven augmentation from them.

The headline comparison is likely invalid. Qwen-Coder-32B-Instruct reaches only 77% valid patches and 18.3% on Verified, and Qwen-Coder-7B-Instruct reaches 6.3% valid patches and 1.3% Pass@1 (Table 10) under the same 'Simplified Agentless' scaffold; the latter is far below any reasonable expectation for that model and strongly indicates the prompt/parse harness is failing for instruct models. The published Agentless protocol with the same 32B instruct model reports substantially higher Verified performance, so the 13.6/12.3 point 'absolute gains over the instruct baseline' that anchor the abstract and contributions are inflated. The meaningful, internally controlled comparison (Base+SFT 11.3 → 24.3) is not what is advertised.

No control for token/compute budget in the multi-language claim. The Python-only setting sees 3.8B mid-training tokens and the 'All Languages' setting 17.7B, both for 2 epochs, so the 22.3 → 24.3 (Lite) and 27.8 → 30.6 (Verified) improvement is fully confounded with 4.7x more training data. There is no mid-training data-scaling curve and no compute-matched control (e.g., continued training on generic permissively licensed code).

The central novelty — verification of the derived Search/Replace blocks — is never ablated. There is no comparison against an unverified S/R conversion, so it is impossible to tell how much of the gain comes from the round-trip verification as opposed to simply using the S/R format with linked issues. Similarly, no ablation on mid-training corpus size, and no ablation on the SFT data scale.

The most important missing baseline is mid-training on existing executable SWE data (SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-smith) at a matched token budget. These datasets are used only in the SFT stage (Table 5), which is precisely where most of the gain materialises (11.3 → 24.3 on Lite), so the paper does not actually demonstrate that PR-derived data fills the claimed gap relative to verification-rich alternatives.

Decontamination is described only for the Clean-PR mid-training corpus. The SFT stage draws trajectories from SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live (and Multi-SWE-bench-RL for multilingual), and the paper never verifies non-overlap of these sources with SWE-bench Lite/Verified. Given that the largest jumps occur after SFT, this is a material reproducibility/validity gap.

Table 7 is not credible as written: Lingma-SWE (72B) and SWE-Fixer (72B) are listed with identical numbers on both splits (22.0/30.2), which looks like a transcription error, and the table compares systems with different base models, different scaffolds, and different training data. The claim that a 32B model 'surpasses the 72B baselines' is therefore unsupported by the evidence presented.

Reproducibility and licensing: the abstract and contributions claim 'the largest publicly available corpus', but the appendix only says the dataset is planned for release, no model checkpoints are mentioned, and Clean-PR apparently applies no licence filtering (the authors' own StarCoder2-style baseline in Appendix B.1 explicitly drops non-permissive/GPL repositories). Releasing PR-derived content, repository URLs, and reviewer comments without licence screening or a PII/username discussion is a real ethical/legal concern that the impact statement does not resolve.

Framing overreach. The paper claims to reduce reliance on 'heavy inference scaffolding', yet evaluation still uses a three-stage pipeline with repository-structure prompts, retrieval, and top-3 file selection (Appendix C), and the fine-tuned models are trained on exactly this decomposition. The intermediate metrics (File Acc., Line Acc., Valid Patch) are therefore partly measures of format alignment with training rather than intrinsic capability, and the 'positive transfer' claim from Figure 2 rests on one run of HumanEval/LiveCodeBench with no control for generic continued pretraining.

Presentation and citation quality are poor: Table 15 contains a corrupted token ('.邮') in every row's allowed-extension list; references have mismatched years and duplicates (He et al. 2014 cited as 2025; Hui et al. 2025 vs. 2024; Zeng et al. 2023 vs. 2025 with an implausible arXiv ID; Johnson et al. 2019 cited as 2021; two entries labelled 'Zhang et al. [2023]'); Table 8's 'Description' column header is ambiguous; and the corpus size is inconsistently stated (2M in the abstract vs. 3.05M in Table 1).

Limitations are under-discussed. Appendix D mentions only the ≤5-core-files filter and long-context/multi-architecture extensions; it does not acknowledge the absence of seeds, the token-budget confound, the instruct-baseline anomaly, or the licensing gap.

strengths: Provides a genuinely valuable, large-scale resource: a 2M-PR, 12-language, 17.7B-token verified corpus (Clean-PR), with a principled pipeline (Algorithm 1) that reconstructs the post-PR state via 'fake git apply', derives minimal unique Search/Replace blocks, and discards any example that does not round-trip bit-wise. This directly targets a real gap between noisy PR traces and rigorous repo-editing supervision.

Clean, well-controlled ablations isolate the contribution of each design choice: a matched-token-budget StarCoder2-style baseline (17.4B vs 17.7B) shows the data-construction gain (15.7 -> 24.3 on Lite; 20.4 -> 30.6 on Verified), and separate ablations confirm the value of the Search/Replace format (27.8 vs 24.4 on Verified), linked-issue augmentation (27.8 vs 25.7), and error-driven augmentation (27.4 -> 30.6).

Decontamination is unusually thorough and actively tests the leakage hypothesis: repository exclusion, SHA-256 file matching, 15-gram code filtering, and issue Jaccard filtering, plus a semantic-leakage quintile analysis (most-similar quintile has the lowest resolve rate, r=-0.061, p=0.184). This is exactly the kind of evidence that strengthens the causal claim.

Broad generalisation evidence strengthens the paper beyond a single benchmark: 7B scale (10.3 -> 14.5 on Lite), multilingual Multi-SWE-bench (7.0 -> 12.3), transfer to OpenHands CodeActAgent (16.1 -> 20.7 on Lite), and a catastrophic-forgetting analysis showing positive rather than negative transfer on HumanEval/LiveCodeBench.
The data pipeline, prompt templates, and release schema are documented in detail (Appendices A-C), supporting reproducibility of the method itself.
weaknesses: The headline 'surpasses 72B baselines' claim is not decisive: Table 7 lists Lingma-SWE and SWE-Fixer with identical numbers (22.0/30.2), which appears to be a copy/transcription error, and the margins (24.3 vs 22.0 on Lite; 30.6 vs 30.2 on Verified) are within plausible run-to-run noise.

No variance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported for any Pass@1 number. With only 300/500 instances, several reported differences (e.g., 20.4 vs 19.1 on Lite; 30.6 vs 30.2 in Table 7) cannot be reliably distinguished from noise, yet the paper draws firm conclusions from them.

Decontamination of the SFT trajectories against SWE-bench Lite/Verified is not explicitly established. The paper states non-overlap only for the Multi-SWE-bench-RL set, but the main SWE-bench results use SWE-Gym / SWE-rebench / SWE-bench-Live trajectories whose overlap status with the evaluation splits is not reported.

The mid-training vs. SFT distinction is blurry: 'mid-training' is effectively continued instruction tuning on PR edit data, and no experiment holds total compute constant (e.g., training SFT longer) to show that the two-stage schedule itself, rather than simply more tokens, drives the gain.

The StarCoder2-style baseline is weaker by construction (unified diff format, retains config artifacts, no issue augmentation), so part of the headline gap reflects deliberate baseline design choices rather than only data quality; the paper's own ablations partially acknowledge this but the framing overstates the comparison.

The error-driven augmentation generates hard negatives with Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, which is also the zero-shot baseline, creating a somewhat circular dependency, and the quality/diversity of these negatives is not analysed.
The dataset is only promised ('we plan to release'), so full reproducibility is deferred, and the 'largest publicly available corpus' claim is prospective rather than verifiable at review time.
